readerTitle: Nobody buys a game console for the box
caseNote: 실제 관찰 (게임기 구매 장면, 게임기 업계의 일반적 수익 구조) + 실제 기업 (Nintendo, 1983년 북미 게임 시장 붕괴 이후) + 가상 적용 (푸드홀, 디자인 앱 플러그인 마켓)
insight: 게임기 회사는 기계가 아니라 그 위에 올라갈 게임(보완재)을 관리하는 사업을 한다. 보완재를 늘리는 일과 문을 지키는 일을 함께 해야 플랫폼이 산다.
misconception: 게임기 경쟁은 더 빠른 칩, 더 좋은 기계를 만드는 쪽이 이긴다.

sources.text: Nintendo, company history: Official Nintendo Seal of Quality and licensing program for the NES (mid-1980s)
The 1983 North American video game crash, widely documented in game industry histories
게임기 하드웨어를 원가 근처나 원가 이하로 팔고 게임 판매와 라이선스 수수료로 버는 구조는 업계의 일반적 관찰
게임기 출시 선택지, 푸드홀, 디자인 앱 플러그인 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: "게임기 회사들이 하드웨어를 원가 근처나 그 이하로 팔아 왔다"는 일반적 서술로만 적었습니다. 특정 회사·기종의 손실 금액은 쓰지 않았습니다. 모든 회사·모든 세대에 해당하지는 않는다는 점(일부 Nintendo 기기는 하드웨어에서도 이익)을 카드에 "often"으로 반영했습니다. 게시 전 표현을 다시 확인하세요.
1983년 북미 게임 시장 붕괴의 원인으로 저품질 게임 범람이 흔히 꼽히지만, 과잉 공급과 가정용 컴퓨터와의 경쟁 등 여러 요인이 있습니다. 카드에는 "one widely cited cause"로 적었습니다.
Nintendo가 NES에서 라이선스 프로그램과 Seal of Quality, 무단 카트리지를 막는 잠금 칩을 도입한 내용은 Nintendo 역사 자료와 업계사로 확인하세요. 서드파티 연간 출시 수 제한 같은 세부 규칙은 확인이 어려워 쓰지 않았습니다.
플러그인 마켓의 30% 수수료와 2주 심사 기간은 가상 설정입니다. 실제 특정 플랫폼의 수수료로 읽히지 않도록 illustrative 표시를 유지하세요.

cards.title: Nobody buys a game console for the box
body: Watch a parent in an electronics store choosing between two consoles. They rarely ask about the processor or the memory.
They ask one question: *which games does my kid want?* The box is just the ticket to those games. That simple fact shapes almost every move a console maker makes.

image.label: A parent and child comparing two game consoles by looking at the game shelf
image.brief: 전자제품 매장. 부모와 아이가 게임기 두 대 앞에 서 있지만 시선은 뒤쪽 게임 진열대를 향함. 게임기 상자는 흐릿하게, 게임 진열대는 선명하게. 실제 게임기 디자인, 로고, 게임 타이틀은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You're launching a new console.
body: Your machine is ready. You have one big budget left before launch and three ways to spend it.
Which gives your console the best chance?

options.text: Upgrade to a faster chip than the rival's
options.feedback: Better hardware helps a little, but few buyers choose on specs. A powerful box with few games is still an empty box.

options.text: Fund studios to make games for it and keep their fees low
options.feedback: This is **complements** at work: games make the console worth owning. More good games raise the value of every machine you sell.

options.text: Cut the launch price by a third
options.feedback: A lower price brings in buyers, and more players attract studios. But without games ready, cheap consoles end up in closets.

cards.title: The library is the product.
body: Games and consoles are **complements**: each is worth more because the other exists. A console's value rises with every good game made for it.

That creates a chicken-and-egg problem. Studios want to build for a console many people own. People want a console with many games. So console makers often pay to break the deadlock: funding early games, building their own, and making it easy for outside studios to join.

cards.title: Cheap box, paid games.
body: Console makers have often sold their hardware at or close to cost, sometimes below it, especially at launch.
They make it back on what goes on top. Each game sold by an outside studio usually pays the console maker a fee. Their own games and online services add more.
A cheap box puts more consoles in homes. More homes attract more studios. More games sell more boxes.

image.label: Money flow: low-margin console, fees from every game sold
image.brief: 순환 다이어그램. 왼쪽 "Console: sold near cost" 작은 동전, 오른쪽 "Every game: a fee to the console maker" 큰 동전 더미. 가운데 화살표 순환 "More players → more studios → more games". 실제 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: Phone and app platforms follow a similar pattern. The platform's value grows with each app built on it, and a share of app sales often flows back to the platform owner.

cards.title: Too many bad games nearly killed the business.
body: In 1983, the North American home game market collapsed. One widely cited cause: shelves flooded with rushed, low-quality games, and buyers stopped trusting any of them.

When Nintendo brought its console to North America a few years later, it acted as a **gatekeeper**. Outside studios needed a license, games carried a *Seal of Quality*, and a chip blocked unlicensed cartridges.
More games help only if buyers can trust them.

cards.title: Now it's a food hall.
body: You're opening a food hall with 12 stalls. Customers come for the mix of food. You earn rent plus a share of each vendor's sales.
Twenty vendors have applied, including six burger stands. How do you fill the stalls?

options.text: Take the first 12 applicants to open on time
options.feedback: You fill stalls fast, but five burger stands compete with each other instead of adding variety. Skipping the **gatekeeper** role lets weak vendors drag down everyone.

options.text: Pick 12 vendors who cover different cuisines and meet a quality bar
options.feedback: Each stall becomes a **complement** to the others, so a group with mixed tastes has a reason to come. Being a careful gatekeeper protects the whole hall.

options.text: Skip outside vendors and run all 12 kitchens yourself
options.feedback: You get full control, but you carry all the cost and risk, and you lose the variety and energy outside vendors bring.

cards.softwareNote: An app store faces the same choice: approving every app fills the shelves fast, but a flood of copycats and scams makes users trust none of them.

cards.title: The gate can be too tight, or too expensive.
body: Gatekeeping protects quality, but outside creators pay for it. If approval is slow, rules are unclear or fees are high, they build somewhere else.

A platform owner can also be tempted to favor its own products over outside ones. Do it too often, and the best partners leave. The goal is a gate that keeps out harm, not one that takes every profit for yourself.

image.label: A narrow gate with a long line of creators turning away
image.brief: 좁은 문 앞에 개발자·요리사·디자이너 캐릭터들이 줄을 서 있고, 일부는 돌아서서 다른 문으로 향함. 문 위에 "Fees", "Slow review" 표지판. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Now it's a design app.
body: Your design app has a plugin marketplace. Outside developers build plugins and you take 30% of their sales. Review takes two weeks.
Top developers say they may move to a rival app. What do you change?

options.text: Keep the review, make it faster, and lower the fee for small developers
options.feedback: You keep the **gatekeeper** role that protects users from broken or unsafe plugins, while making it cheaper to build the **complements** that keep users with you.

options.text: Drop the review entirely so plugins launch instantly
options.feedback: Developers would love the speed, but one harmful plugin could cost users' trust in all of them. The 1983 lesson applies here too.

options.text: Hold firm. Users are here, so developers will stay
options.feedback: Users stay partly because of the plugins. Push their makers away and the complements leave first, then the users.

cards.title: Run the box to grow what goes on it.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Complements:** the console is worth what its games are worth, so grow the library. **Gatekeepers:** control who gets in, so customers can trust what they find, without driving creators away.
**Try it today:** list what customers use alongside your product. Which one would you make cheaper or easier to get, and who decides what's allowed in?
